Orthonormality is a special case of [[orthogonality]].

== Mathematical definition ==

Let [[vector space]] $V$ be an [[inner product space]].

If for $u,v\in V$

$$
\begin{cases}
\langle u, v \rangle=0 & \text{(orthogonality)} \\
\langle u, u \rangle=1 \land \langle v, v \rangle=1 & \text{(normality)}
\end{cases}
$$

Then $u,v$ are '''orthonormal''' to each other.
<ref>{{#cite:Q1930}}</ref>

== Orthonormal vector list ==

A list of '''nonzero''' vectors $(e_1,\ldots,e_m) \in V$ is '''orthonormal''' if

$$
\langle e_i, e_j \rangle = \delta_{i,j} \Leftarrow i,j \in \{1,m\}
$$

where $\delta_{ij}$ is the [[Kronecker delta function]], i.e., $\delta_{ij} = \text{ if } i=j \text{ otherwise } 0$.

which means:

$$
\langle e_i, e_j \rangle = 0 \Leftarrow 1\le i\neq j \le m & \text{(orthogonality)}\\
\langle e_i, e_i \rangle = 1 \Leftarrow 1\le i \le m & \text{(normality)}
$$

== Orthonormal basis ==

Any [[#orthonormal vector list|orthonormal vector list]] of length $dim(V)$ is an '''orthonormal basis''' for $V$.<ref>{{#cite:Q1930}}</ref>

Which means:

If $(e_1,\ldots,e_n)$ is an orthonormal vector list for $V \in \mathbb{F}^n$

Then

$$
\forall v = a_1 e_1 + \cdots + a_n e_n
$$

=== Property ===

$$
\forall v\in V
\begin{cases}
v=\sum_{k=1}^n \langle v,e_k\rangle e_k \\
\lVert v\rVert^2=\sum_{k=1}^n |\langle v,e_k\rangle|^2
\end{cases}
$$

{{Hidden proof}}
$$
\because v = a_1 e_1 + \cdots + a_n e_n & \text{(1)} \\
\therefore \forall k \in \{1, \cdots, n\}, \langle v, e_k \rangle= \langle a_1 e_1 + \cdots + a_n e_n , e_k \rangle = a_k \\
\therefore \text{(1) becomes } v =  \langle v, e_1 \rangle e_1 + \cdots + \langle v, e_n \rangle e_n \\
\text{i.e., } v=\sum_{k=1}^n \langle v,e_k\rangle e_k \\
$$

and

$$
\lVert v\rVert^2=\sum_{k=1}^n |a_k|^2=\sum_{k=1}^n |\langle v,e_k\rangle|^2
$$
{{End hidden}}
